name: KnowledgeEditor

paper.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models

construction.unit: one revision (input x, old prediction y, new prediction a) written into the LM's weights
construction.kept_as: a weight shift Δθ predicted by a hyper-network; no text is stored
construction.processing: a BiLSTM encodes the revision; per weight matrix, small FFNN heads turn that code and the gradient of the loss on a into ΔW
construction.writer: trained hyper-network (54M parameters for BERT, 67M for BART)

organization.structure: none: the fact is spread over the LM's weight matrices

management.operations: one additive update θ' = θ + Δθ per edit; the +loop variant re-applies it until the prediction flips
management.conflicts: editor trained under a KL limit so outputs on other inputs stay the same; edits are evaluated one at a time, never stacked

retrieval.candidates: none: the model reads its parameters

use.context: the input alone; the revised fact is read from the edited weights
use.reasoning: one forward pass; beam search (5 beams in code) for QA, sign of the logit for fact-checking

classify.note: Parametric memory: an edit changes the LM's weights and every later query reads them in one forward pass; there is no store to search.

stages.ingestion: An edit request names an input x, the model's current prediction y and the desired prediction a.
stages.construction: A hyper-network encodes the request with a BiLSTM and, for each weight matrix, combines that code with the gradient of the loss on a to predict a weight shift ΔW.
stages.update: The shift is added to the weights once (θ' = θ + Δθ); an optional test-time loop re-applies it until the prediction changes.
stages.answer: Every later query is answered by the edited model directly from its parameters.
stages.learning: The hyper-network is trained once per model by constrained optimization: raise the likelihood of a (and optionally of paraphrases of x) while keeping the KL divergence on other inputs below an annealed margin, solved with a Lagrange multiplier.

summary: Learned knowledge editor: a hyper-network turns one fact revision and its gradient into a weight update for BERT or BART, trained to change that fact and its paraphrases while keeping all other predictions fixed.
notes:
VENUE: EMNLP 2021 main (Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing; aclanthology 2021.emnlp-main.522). arXiv comment says 'Accepted at EMNLP2021' but then names the 2020 proceedings; the ACL Anthology page confirms 2021. Text read from arXiv v2 (2021-09-08).
SCOPE: memory here is the LM's parameters, not an external store. Each edit is evaluated on its own starting from the original model; the paper does not test sequences of edits.
RESULTS: all four metrics go in category with metric 'other' (they are accuracies except performance deterioration, a relative drop where lower is better). QA equivalence accuracy has two numbers (generated / human paraphrases), kept as two categories.

sources.code_note: Latest commit (2022-01-28, 'Fix #4'); the later commits only touch the README, requirements and a small fix; the model and training code date from 2021 (e.g. commit 668aca6d, 2021-08-25). It is the repository linked in the paper.

headline: The 'memory' being edited is the LM's weights; nothing is stored outside the model and nothing is retrieved.
One learned network writes each edit as a single weight update; a KL limit during its training is what keeps other predictions unchanged.
Every edit is scored alone on a fresh copy of the original model, so the results say nothing about many edits in a row.

abstract.text: Language models hold facts in their weights, and some of those facts are wrong or go out of date. KnowledgeEditor fixes a single fact without retraining: a hyper-network, given the fact to change and the model's gradient, predicts a weight update. It is trained with a constraint that keeps the model's output distribution on other inputs unchanged, and optionally with paraphrases so that equivalent questions change too. The authors test it on a BERT fact-checker (FEVER) and a BART closed-book QA model (zsRE) and find the updates concentrate in a few components.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

units.name: Edit
units.role: one fact revision applied to the model

fields.name: condition text
fields.what: the revision written as 'y >> a || x' (old prediction, new prediction, input) and read by the BiLSTM

fields.name: gradient
fields.what: gradient of the loss of a on x for every weight matrix of the frozen LM

fields.name: weight shift Δθ
fields.what: σ(η)·(α̂∘∇W + β̂) per matrix, with α̂ and β̂ rank-one outer products; added to every matrix except biases, norms and embeddings
fields.src: paper §4 Eq. 3; code one_shot_learner.py L35-L69, bart_seq2seq_augmented_kilt.py L75-L100

write.how: BiLSTM (hidden 128 per direction) over 'y >> a || x', then an FFNN to a 1,024-dim vector h
write.src: paper App. B.5; code one_shot_learner.py L72-L105

write.how: backpropagate the loss of the new prediction a on x through the frozen LM
per weight matrix, an FFNN on h gives α, β, γ, δ, η; ΔW = σ(η)·(softmax outer product ∘ gradient + bias term)

write.out: success rate 98.80 (FC) / 94.65 (QA) with a single update

write.how: minimize the loss on a (and on paraphrases for +Px) plus α·(KL on the rest of the mini-batch - margin); α is updated by gradient ascent and clipped at 0; margin ×0.8 whenever > 90% of validation edits succeed
write.src: paper §4, App. A, B.6; code bart_seq2seq_augmented_kilt.py L245-L283, L411-L436

read.scores: nothing is matched; the query runs through the edited weights
read.how: QA: beam search, top-1 (5 beams in code); FC: positive logit means 'true'
if the prediction is still not a, add the same Δθ again; test time only
read.src: paper §6.1, Table 1 †; code bart_seq2seq_augmented_kilt.py L369-L404, eval_bart_seq2seq.py L255-L265

answer_context.sees: only the query; the edited fact is in the weights
answer_context.format: plain model input (claim for FC, question for QA)
excludes: paraphrases (used only in training and scoring)

compression.what: stored edit vs the fact it encodes
compression.basis: Not applicable in token terms: an edit is a dense shift over all weight matrices of a 110M (BERT) or 139M (BART) model, produced by a 54M / 67M-parameter editor (App. B.5).

numbers.label: Base model accuracy
numbers.value: BERT on FEVER 77.1%; BART on zsRE 22.1% exact match

numbers.label: Chance full KE beats all baselines
numbers.value: ≈97% FC, ≈88% QA over 1,000 random metric weightings

numbers.label: Editor without the gradient input
numbers.value: FC ≈10x slower to converge; QA did not converge

paper_vs_code.code: centered RMSprop with the same learning rates

paper_vs_code.paper: stop on success or after at most 100 gradient steps
paper_vs_code.code: eval scripts loop until the prediction flips, with no step limit

paper_vs_code.paper: updates are applied in a loop until success (up to a maximum), affecting all metrics
paper_vs_code.code: the loop runs only when scoring paraphrases; success and retain use the single update (the looped Δθ is discarded), unlike the FEVER script

paper_vs_code.paper: five FFNNs [1024, tanh, d] per weight matrix
paper_vs_code.code: one FFNN per matrix (1,024 → 128, tanh → output) whose output is split into the five vectors
FC script: batch 256, 50k steps on 1 GPU; QA script: batch 64 on 4 GPUs, 200k steps

open_questions: Edits are never accumulated, so whether retain accuracy holds after tens or thousands of edits is untested.
Retain accuracy compares against the model's own old predictions, not gold answers, so it rewards stability rather than correctness.
Alternative QA answers are other beam hypotheses of the same model, which may be easier targets than arbitrary new facts.

discussion.takeaway: A small learned editor can rewrite one fact in a fine-tuned LM with a single weight update, keeping about 98% of other predictions, whereas fine-tuning or norm-constrained fine-tuning trades success, stability and paraphrase consistency against each other.

claims.claim: KnowledgeEditor meets all three desiderata at once, unlike the baselines.
claims.evidence: FC 98.80 success / 98.14 retain / 82.69 equiv.; QA 94.65 / 98.73 / 86.50; probability of beating all baselines ≈97% (FC) and ≈88% (QA). Table 1, Fig. 6

claims.claim: A constraint in function space (KL) is needed; one in parameter space is not enough.
claims.evidence: With an L2 constraint retain accuracy falls to 45.10 (FC) and 46.66 (QA). Table 1, §6.2

claims.claim: Training with paraphrases improves consistency without hurting success or retain.
Fine-tuning either forgets or does not generalize.
claims.evidence: All layers: retain 86.95 FC / 67.55 QA; 1st layer on FC: equivalence 42.24. Table 1, §6.1

claims.claim: Edits concentrate in a few components, unlike gradients or fine-tuning.
claims.evidence: Update magnitudes, Fig. 4, §6.4; low cosine similarity with fine-tuning updates, App. C Table 2

limits: The editor is trained for a single update; applying several in sequence is left to future work.
The same tool could be used to insert false facts into a model.
discussion.limits_src: paper §6.1 fn. 8, Ethical Considerations (no separate limitations section)
reading: Every edit starts from the original model and is scored alone, so the setting is one fact at a time, not a growing memory.
The edited models are small fine-tuned classifiers and QA models (BERT-base, BART-base with 22.1% zsRE accuracy), and the new QA answers are the model's own lower-ranked beam hypotheses.

Baselines stop only on success (fine-tuning) or after a hyperparameter search that includes retain accuracy (Zhu et al.); KnowledgeEditor without the loop gets one update, so success rates are not measured under equal budgets.
The paper states Adam and a 100-step cap for fine-tuning; the released code uses RMSprop for the editor and has no step cap, and its QA eval applies +loop only to paraphrases.
